fields.title: Ecclesiastes
fields.subtitle: Qohelet, “The one who gathers”
fields.description: The Bible’s most honest book about the limits of life, spoken by the Teacher, a king in Jerusalem who tried wisdom, pleasure, great works and wealth, and found that “Everything is a breath.” The sun rises and sets, the wind goes round, the wise die like fools and the righteous sometimes perish, and no one can see the whole of what God is doing. Yet again and again the Teacher turns to say that bread and wine, work and love are gifts from the hand of God, to be received with joy. A time for everything under the heavens, a cord of three strands, bread sent out on the waters, “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth”, and the end of the matter: fear God and keep his commandments. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Ecclesiastes about?
qa.answer: Ecclesiastes is a search for what lasts. Its speaker, the Teacher, tests wisdom, pleasure, great works, wealth and long life to see what anyone gains from all their hard work “under the sun”, and finds that everything is hevel, a breath: brief, beyond grasping, and leaving no lasting profit. He faces injustice, loneliness and above all death, which comes to the wise and the foolish alike. Yet seven times he commends joy, the simple goods of food, work and love received as God’s gift, and the book ends: “Fear God and keep his commandments, because this is the whole of being human” (12:13).

qa.question: Who wrote Ecclesiastes?
qa.answer: The book calls its speaker Qohelet, “the one who gathers” an assembly, translated “the Preacher” in older Bibles and “the Teacher” here, and introduces him as “David’s son, king in Jerusalem” (1:1). It never gives his name. Jewish and Christian tradition long received the book as Solomon’s, and chapter 2 recalls his wisdom, building and wealth. Many scholars, noting that its Hebrew is among the latest in the Bible, think a later sage wrote it in Solomon’s person, perhaps in the fifth to third centuries BC. A second voice frames the Teacher’s words at the beginning and the end (1:1–2; 12:8–14).

qa.question: What does “vanity of vanities” mean?
qa.answer: It is the traditional English rendering of the book’s opening cry (1:2). The Hebrew word, hevel, used nearly forty times in Ecclesiastes, means a breath or a puff of vapour, the breath you see on a cold morning, real and then gone. It is also the name of Abel. The Teacher uses it of what is brief, of what cannot be grasped or understood, and of what comes to nothing. “Vanity” once meant emptiness but now suggests conceit, and “meaningless” keeps only one of its senses, so this translation keeps the picture: “Breath upon breath, says the Teacher, breath upon breath! Everything is a breath.” The doubled form is a Hebrew superlative, like “Song of Songs”.

qa.question: Is Ecclesiastes a pessimistic book?
qa.answer: Readers have long debated it. The Teacher speaks bluntly about injustice, the shortness of life and death, and sets sayings side by side that seem to pull against each other: sorrow is better than laughter (7:3), yet eat your bread with joy (9:7). Some read him as a man of faith clearing away false hopes so that only God and his gifts remain; some as an honest sceptic whose doubts the closing frame answers; some as a deliberate portrait of how life looks “under the sun”, set in Scripture to point the reader higher. What is clear is that God is present throughout the book, that joy is repeatedly commended as his gift, and that the book ends in the fear of God and the certainty of his judgment.

qa.question: What does “a time for everything” mean in Ecclesiastes 3?
qa.answer: Ecclesiastes 3:1–8 is a poem of fourteen pairs — a time to give birth and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to root up, a time to cry and a time to laugh, a time for war and a time for peace — which says that every matter under the heavens has its set time. It is both a comfort and a humbling: our times come to us, and we do not choose them. A few verses later the Teacher adds that God “has made everything fitting in its own time” and “put a sense of eternity in their hearts”, though no one can discover the whole of his work (3:11).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Its poems are set line by line, and the book’s keyword is rendered “breath” throughout. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Breath upon breath, says the Teacher, breath upon breath! Everything is a breath.

— Ecclesiastes 1:2

There is no other book in the Bible quite like this one. It opens with a cry that sounds almost like despair, and it closes with the same cry. In between, a king who has tried everything reports on what he found: that wisdom does not save the wise from dying, that pleasure leaves the heart empty, that the hard work of a lifetime passes to someone who never lifted a finger for it, and that the righteous sometimes perish while the wicked live long. He does not look away from any of it.

And yet this book is Scripture. Generations of readers have found it the most honest voice in the Bible, the one that says aloud what they had been afraid to think. In the synagogue it is read at the Feast of Booths, the most joyful festival of the year, as if to say that joy is safest in the hands of those who know how brief life is. For Ecclesiastes is not finally a book of despair. Again and again, in the middle of its hardest chapters, it stops to say that bread and wine and work and love are gifts from the hand of God, to be received with gladness while there is time.

“The one who gathers”

The speaker of the book is called Qohelet, a word found nowhere else in the Bible. It comes from the Hebrew for an assembly, and means one who gathers people together and speaks to them; he also gathered and arranged wise sayings (12:9). The ancient Greek translation rendered it Ekklesiastes, a member or leader of the assembly, and that gave the book its English name. Older Bibles call him “the Preacher”. This translation calls him “the Teacher”, because, as the book says at its end, he “taught the people knowledge”.

He is introduced as “David’s son, king in Jerusalem”, and in chapter 2 he describes houses and vineyards, gardens and pools, silver and gold, singers and slaves, greater than all who were before him in Jerusalem. Readers have always heard Solomon in this, and Jewish and Christian tradition long received the book as his, written in old age. But the book never gives his name, and many scholars, noticing that its Hebrew is among the latest in the Bible, think a later sage wrote it, taking on Solomon’s place in order to test where wisdom, pleasure and wealth lead. Christians hold both views. Either way, the voice is that of someone who has had everything a person could want, and so can tell you what it is worth.

Two voices

Listen carefully and you will hear two voices in the book. Most of it is Qohelet speaking for himself, “I, the Teacher”. But the first verses speak about him from outside, “says the Teacher”, and so do the last ones, from 12:8 to the end. Once, in the middle, the outer voice breaks in again (7:27). Someone has framed the Teacher’s words, introduced him and then, at the close, commented on him:

Besides being wise, the Teacher also taught the people knowledge. He weighed and studied and arranged many proverbs. The Teacher sought to find pleasing words, and to write honestly words of truth.

— Ecclesiastes 12:9–10

The frame does not argue with the Teacher or soften what he said. It honours him as wise and honest, and then it has the last word. That last word, as we shall see, is the key to reading the whole.

“Breath upon breath”

The book’s keyword is hevel, used nearly forty times. Older Bibles translate it “vanity”, which once meant emptiness but now suggests conceit; some newer ones say “meaningless”. But the word is a picture. Hevel is a breath, the puff of vapour you see on a cold morning, real enough and then gone. It is also the name of Abel, whose life was over almost as soon as it began.

The Teacher uses the picture in more than one way. Sometimes he means that a thing is brief: life is “a mere breath, which they pass like a shadow” (6:12). Sometimes he means that it cannot be grasped or understood, as when the righteous get what the wicked deserve (8:14). And sometimes he means that it comes to nothing, that all the effort leaves no lasting gain. This translation keeps the picture, so that the word can carry all three senses: “Everything is a breath.”

Beside it stand two other refrains. One is “chasing the wind”, the effort to catch what will not be caught. The other is the question the book asks in its third verse:

What do people gain from all the hard work they do under the sun?

— Ecclesiastes 1:3

The word for “gain” is a word from bookkeeping. It means what is left over when the accounts are done. The Teacher is not asking whether work achieves anything at all. He is asking whether anything remains to a person in the end.

Under the sun

The Hebrew phrase “under the sun” comes twenty-nine times in Ecclesiastes and nowhere else in the Old Testament. It marks out the field of the Teacher’s search: life as anyone on earth can see and test it, where the sun rises and sets and hurries back to rise again. He looks at the world as it is, without leaning on a heavenly answer before he has faced the earthly question.

That does not make him an unbeliever. God is everywhere in the book: it is God who has given human beings their task, God who makes everything fitting in its time, God who will judge, God whose gifts are bread and joy. What the Teacher refuses to do is pretend that the ways of God are easy to read. The book always calls him simply “God”, never by his personal name, the LORD, as if to keep him at the distance from which he is seen “under the sun”.

The great experiment

In 1:12–2:26 the Teacher tells how he set out to find what is good for human beings “during the few days of their lives”. He tried wisdom and found that “with much wisdom comes much vexation”. He tried pleasure and laughter and wine. He built and planted and gathered treasure, and denied himself nothing. Then he took stock:

Then I looked at all that my hands had done and at the hard work I had spent in doing it, and I found that everything was a breath and chasing the wind. Nothing was gained under the sun.

— Ecclesiastes 2:11

Wisdom is better than folly, he grants, as light is better than darkness. “Yet I also came to know that one fate comes to them all” (2:14). The wise die like fools and are forgotten like them. What a person builds goes to the next owner, “And who knows whether that one will be wise or a fool?” (2:19). The experiment ends in the bleakest words of the book: “So I hated life.”

And then, at once, comes the first of the book’s turns:

There is nothing better for people than to eat and drink and find enjoyment in their hard work. This too, I saw, comes from the hand of God.

— Ecclesiastes 2:24

The pattern repeats through the book. The Teacher goes down into the hard facts, and comes up with the same quiet counsel: receive the day and its work and its food as God’s gift.

A time for everything

The best-known passage in Ecclesiastes is a poem of fourteen pairs, from birth and death to war and peace:

There is a set time for everything, a time for every matter under the heavens: a time to give birth, a time to die, a time to plant, a time to root up what was planted, a time to kill, a time to heal, a time to pull down, a time to build up, a time to cry, a time to laugh, a time to lament, a time to dance, a time to scatter stones, a time to gather stones, a time to embrace, a time to hold back from embracing, a time to search, a time to give up as lost, a time to keep, a time to throw away, a time to tear, a time to stitch together, a time to stay silent, a time to speak, a time to love, a time to hate, a time for war, a time for peace.

— Ecclesiastes 3:1–8

It is often read as a comfort, and it is one. But it is also humbling. We do not choose our times; they are set, and they come to us. The Teacher draws the lesson a few verses later, in one of the deepest sentences in the book:

God has made everything fitting in its own time. He has also put a sense of eternity in their hearts, but people still cannot discover the work God has done from start to finish.

— Ecclesiastes 3:11

Human beings are made for more than the moment. We carry a sense of eternity, and so we cannot be satisfied by what passes. Yet we cannot see the whole of what God is doing. Ecclesiastes lives inside that tension, and it does not pretend to resolve it.

What the Teacher saw

The middle chapters move from one observation to the next, often in short sayings like those in Proverbs. He sees “the tears of the oppressed, with no one to comfort them” (4:1). He sees a man working endlessly with no one to work for: “For whom am I working so hard,” he asks, “and going without anything good?” (4:8). He sees that “Two are better than one”, and that “a cord of three strands does not snap quickly” (4:9, 12). He sees that “Whoever loves money never has enough money” (5:10), and that we leave the world as we entered it, “naked as he came” (5:15).

Most of all he sees death, which comes to all alike. “It is the same for everyone: one fate comes to the righteous and the wicked” (9:2). He even says that “a living dog is better off than a dead lion” (9:4). The Teacher does not have the resurrection to set against the grave. He looks at death squarely, and lets it teach him how to live. “It is better to go to a house of mourning than to go to a house of feasting,” he says, “because death is the end of everyone, and the living will take it to heart” (7:2).

Before God, few words

In the middle of the book comes a short passage on worship, and it is characteristic of the Teacher. He does not warn against too little religion but against careless religion: rash vows, hurried words, sacrifices offered by people who do not listen:

Watch your step when you go to the house of God. Coming near to listen is better than offering a sacrifice as fools do, for they do not know that they are doing wrong. Do not speak rashly, and do not let your heart be quick to say anything before God. God is in heaven and you are on earth, so keep your words few.

— Ecclesiastes 5:1–2

The passage ends with the counsel that runs beneath the whole book: “For when dreams and words are many, they are only a breath. Instead, fear God” (5:7).

Joy as a gift

Seven times the Teacher stops to commend joy (2:24–26; 3:12–13; 3:22; 5:18–20; 8:15; 9:7–10; 11:7–10), and each time it comes more strongly. By chapter 9 it has become a command:

Go, eat your food with joy, and drink your wine with a glad heart, for God has already approved what you do.

— Ecclesiastes 9:7

He goes on: wear white, enjoy life with the one you love, and “Whatever your hand finds to do, put all your strength into it” (9:10). This is not the shrug of those who say, “Let us eat and drink, since tomorrow we die” (1 Corinthians 15:32). It is a man who has seen through every attempt to make life pay a lasting profit, and has found that the ordinary goods of food and work and love are still good, because God gives them. The breath is brief. That is why it is precious.

The book’s tensions

Ecclesiastes often sets sayings side by side that seem to pull against each other. Sorrow is better than laughter (7:3), yet eat your bread with joy (9:7). Wisdom gains more than folly, yet the wise die like fools. Toil is a breath, yet it is a gift. “Do not be too righteous,” he says, “and do not make yourself too wise” (7:16), and in the next breath, “Do not be too wicked.” Readers have puzzled over these tensions for centuries.

They have read the book in different ways. Some hear in the Teacher a man of faith clearing away false hopes, so that only God and his gifts are left. Some hear an honest sceptic whose doubts the frame answers at the end. Some hear a deliberate portrait of how life looks “under the sun”, set in Scripture to drive the reader to look higher. There is truth in each. What all agree on is that the tensions belong to the book. They are part of how it teaches, and a reader who smooths them away too quickly will miss what it has to say.

“Remember your Creator”

The last poem of the Teacher is addressed to the young: “Be glad, young man, while you are young” (11:9). But it goes on, “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth”, and then paints, in a series of images, the coming of age and death. The guards of the house tremble, the women who grind stop because they are few, the windows grow dim, the almond tree blossoms. Many readers have heard in these pictures the failing body: trembling hands, few teeth, dim eyes, white hair. Then the silver cord snaps, the golden bowl breaks, “and the dust goes back to the earth it came from, and the spirit returns to God, who gave it” (12:7).

And the Teacher’s last words are his first: “Breath upon breath, says the Teacher. Everything is a breath.”

Ecclesiastes and the New Testament

The New Testament never clearly quotes Ecclesiastes, but it answers it. When Paul writes that “Creation was made subject to futility” (Romans 8:20), he uses the Greek word by which the ancient translation rendered the Teacher’s “breath”, and he adds what the Teacher could not see: that creation itself will be set free and share the glory of God’s children. Jesus’s parable of the rich fool, who stores up his harvest and dies that night, ends with the Teacher’s own question: “And the things you have made ready, whose will they be then?” (Luke 12:20).

And to the question of 1:3, what anyone gains from all their hard work, Paul gives an answer grounded in the resurrection of Christ. After a long chapter on the risen body, he ends: “in the Lord your hard work is never wasted” (1 Corinthians 15:58). Under the sun, everything is a breath. In the Lord, nothing done for him is lost.

How to read Ecclesiastes

Ecclesiastes is short, and it is best read straight through, in one or two sittings, so that you hear its refrains and feel its turns. A few suggestions:

  • Do not lift out a verse on its own. Many of the Teacher’s sayings are answered a few verses later, and the book means them to be heard together.
  • Listen for the refrains. “Breath”, “under the sun”, “chasing the wind”, and the repeated “There is nothing better”.
  • Read the ending carefully. The frame’s last words (12:9–14) tell you how to hold everything before them.
  • Read it beside Proverbs and Job. Proverbs says how life usually goes; Job and Ecclesiastes take up the times when it does not. Each needs the others.
  • Let it do its work. Ecclesiastes strips away the things we lean on, so that we lean on God. It is not comfortable reading, but it is good medicine.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Ecclesiastes moves between prose and poetry; its poems, such as the round of nature in 1:4–11, the times and seasons of 3:1–8 and the closing poem of age in 12:1–7, are printed one line per line, as the Hebrew sets them out. A few of its choices are worth knowing before you begin.

“Breath.” The book’s keyword hevel is rendered “breath” throughout, not “vanity” or “meaningless”, so that its picture of something real but brief and beyond grasping stays in view. The opening cry piles breath on breath, as the Hebrew does: “Breath upon breath”.

“The Teacher.” The speaker’s Hebrew title, Qohelet, is translated by what he does, “the Teacher”, with a capital because it is the name the book calls him by.

The refrains. “Under the sun” and “chasing the wind” are kept word for word wherever they stand, and the book’s two other key words keep one English word each: “gain”, for what is left over, and “hard work”, for the toil that wears a person out.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Ecclesiastes 1
fields.body_html:
Breath upon breath

These are the words of the Teacher, David’s son, king in Jerusalem. Breath upon breath, says the Teacher, breath upon breath! Everything is a breath. What do people gain from all the hard work they do under the sun?
One generation goes and another comes,
but the earth remains forever.
The sun rises and the sun sets,
and it hurries back, panting, to the place where it rises again.
It blows to the south and turns to the north,
round and round goes the wind,
and on its rounds the wind comes back again.
All the streams run to the sea,
yet the sea is never full;
to the place where the streams run,
there they keep on running.
Everything is wearisome,
more than anyone can say;
the eye is never satisfied with seeing,
and the ear is never filled with hearing.
What has been is what will be,
and what has been done is what will be done;
there is nothing new under the sun.
Is there anything of which people say, “Look, this is new”?
It was already here long ages before us.
No one remembers those who came before,
and those who are yet to come
will not be remembered by those who come after them.

The Teacher searches out wisdom

I, the Teacher, was king over Israel in Jerusalem. I set my mind to seek and to search out by wisdom all that is done under the heavens. It is a miserable task that God has given human beings to keep them busy. I have seen all the deeds that are done under the sun, and I found that everything is a breath and chasing the wind. What is twisted cannot be straightened, and what is missing cannot be counted. I said to myself, “I have gained more and more wisdom, more than all who were over Jerusalem before me, and my mind has taken in a great deal of wisdom and knowledge.” So I set my mind to know wisdom, and to know madness and folly. I came to see that this too is chasing the wind. For with much wisdom comes much vexation, and whoever adds to knowledge adds to pain.

fields.title: Ecclesiastes 2
fields.body_html:
Testing pleasure and great works

I said to myself, “Come, let me try you out with pleasure; enjoy what is good.” But this too was a breath. I said of laughter, “It is madness,” and of pleasure, “What good does it do?” I explored with my mind how to cheer my body with wine, while my mind still guided me with wisdom, and how to take up folly, until I could see what is good for human beings to do under the heavens during the few days of their lives. I undertook great works. I built houses for myself and planted vineyards for myself. I made gardens and parks for myself and planted all kinds of fruit trees in them. I made myself pools of water to irrigate a forest of growing trees. I bought male and female slaves, and I had slaves born in my household. I also owned more herds and flocks than anyone who had been before me in Jerusalem. I amassed silver and gold, and the treasure of kings and provinces. I got myself male and female singers, and what people delight in most: many concubines. So I became great, greater than all who were before me in Jerusalem, and my wisdom stayed with me. I did not keep from my eyes anything they desired, and I did not refuse my heart any pleasure. My heart took pleasure in all my hard work, and this was my share for all my hard work. Then I looked at all that my hands had done and at the hard work I had spent in doing it, and I found that everything was a breath and chasing the wind. Nothing was gained under the sun. Then I turned to look at wisdom, and at madness and folly. For what can the one who comes after the king do? Only what has already been done. And I saw that there is more gain in wisdom than in folly, just as there is more gain in light than in darkness. The wise have eyes in their heads, but the fool walks in the dark. Yet I also came to know that one fate comes to them all. Then I said to myself, “What happens to the fool will happen to me too. So why have I been so wise?” And I said to myself that this too is a breath. For the wise will not be remembered forever, any more than the fool, since in the days to come all will be long forgotten. See how the wise die, just like fools! So I hated life, because what is done under the sun weighed on me; everything is a breath and chasing the wind. I hated all the hard work I had done under the sun, because I must leave what it earned to the one who comes after me. And who knows whether that one will be wise or a fool? Yet he will be master of all that I worked for and gained by wisdom under the sun. This too is a breath. So I turned and gave my heart up to despair over all the hard work I had done under the sun. Someone may work with wisdom, knowledge and skill, and then must leave it all as the share of someone who never worked for it. This too is a breath and a great misfortune. What do people get for all their hard work and all the striving of their hearts as they toil under the sun? All their days are pain, and their work is vexation; even at night their minds do not rest. This too is a breath. There is nothing better for people than to eat and drink and find enjoyment in their hard work. This too, I saw, comes from the hand of God. For who can eat or who can find enjoyment apart from me? God gives wisdom, knowledge and joy to the one who pleases him; but to the sinner he gives the task of gathering and storing up, only to hand it over to the one who pleases God. This too is a breath and chasing the wind.

fields.title: Ecclesiastes 3
fields.body_html:
A time for everything

There is a set time for everything,
a time for every matter under the heavens:

a time to give birth, a time to die,
a time to plant, a time to root up what was planted,
a time to kill, a time to heal,
a time to pull down, a time to build up,
a time to cry, a time to laugh,
a time to lament, a time to dance,
a time to scatter stones, a time to gather stones,
a time to embrace, a time to hold back from embracing,
a time to search, a time to give up as lost,
a time to keep, a time to throw away,
a time to tear, a time to stitch together,
a time to stay silent, a time to speak,
a time to love, a time to hate,
a time for war, a time for peace.

The task God has given

What do workers gain from all their hard work? I have seen the task God has given human beings to keep them busy. God has made everything fitting in its own time. He has also put a sense of eternity in their hearts, but people still cannot discover the work God has done from start to finish. I know that there is nothing better for them than to be glad and to do good as long as they live. And also, when anyone eats and drinks and finds enjoyment in all their hard work, it is God’s gift. I know that whatever God does lasts forever; nothing can be added to it and nothing taken from it. God has done this so that people will fear him. Whatever is has already been, and whatever will be has already been; and God seeks out what has gone by. I saw something else under the sun: in the place of justice there was wickedness, and in the place of righteousness there was wickedness. I said to myself, “God will judge both the righteous and the wicked, since every matter has its time, and every deed its time there.” I said to myself about human beings, “God is testing them, to show them that they are only animals.” For what happens to human beings and what happens to animals is the same: one fate comes to them both. As one dies, so does the other. All of them have the same spirit, and humans have no advantage over animals, for everything is a breath. Everything goes to the same place: all came from the dust, and all go back to the dust. Who knows whether the human spirit rises upward and the spirit of the animal goes down into the earth? So I saw that there is nothing better for people than to rejoice in their work, for that is their share. For who can bring them to see what will happen after them?

fields.title: Ecclesiastes 4
fields.body_html:
Tears with no one to comfort

Again I looked at all the oppression that goes on under the sun. I saw the tears of the oppressed, with no one to comfort them. Power was on the side of their oppressors, and there was no one to comfort them. So I counted the dead, who have already died, more fortunate than the living, who are still alive. But better off than both is the one who has never yet existed and has never seen the evil done under the sun. And I saw that all hard work and all skill in work come from people’s envy of one another. This too is a breath and chasing the wind. Fools fold their hands and eat their own flesh. Better one handful with quiet than two handfuls with hard work and chasing the wind. Again I saw something that is a breath under the sun: There is someone all alone, with no son or brother, yet there is no end to all his hard work, and his eyes are never satisfied with wealth. “For whom am I working so hard,” he asks, “and going without anything good?” This too is a breath and a miserable task. Two are better than one, since together they get a good return for their hard work. If one of them falls, the other can help that one up. But woe to anyone who falls alone, with no one else to help them up! And if two lie down together, they keep warm. But how can one keep warm alone? One person alone may be overpowered, but two together can stand up to an attacker, and a cord of three strands does not snap quickly. A young man who is poor but wise is better than an old king who is a fool and will no longer listen to warning. For the young man came out of prison to become king, even though he was born poor in the kingdom he came to rule. I saw all the living who move about under the sun follow the young man, the second one, who would rise in the king’s place. There was no end to all the people he led, yet those who come later will not be glad about him. This too is a breath and chasing the wind.

fields.title: Ecclesiastes 5
fields.body_html:
Let your words be few

Watch your step when you go to the house of God. Coming near to listen is better than offering a sacrifice as fools do, for they do not know that they are doing wrong. Do not speak rashly, and do not let your heart be quick to say anything before God. God is in heaven and you are on earth, so keep your words few. As dreams come when there is much to do, so a fool’s voice comes with many words. When you make a vow to God, do not put off paying it, for he takes no pleasure in fools. Pay what you vow. It is better not to make a vow than to make one and not pay it. Do not let your mouth lead you into sin, and do not tell the messenger, “It was a mistake.” Why should God be angry at what you say and destroy the work of your hands? For when dreams and words are many, they are only a breath. Instead, fear God. If you see the poor oppressed in a province, and justice and right taken away by force, do not be surprised at it. One official watches over another, and still higher ones are over them both. Yet, for all that, a land gains from having a king who cares for its farmed fields. Whoever loves money never has enough money, and whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with what comes in. This too is a breath. When good things increase, so do those who consume them. And what does their owner get from them, except to look at them? Workers sleep sweetly, whether they eat little or much, but the rich have so much that they cannot sleep. I have seen a painful misfortune under the sun: wealth hoarded by its owner to the owner’s own harm. Then that wealth is lost through some bad venture, and when he has a son, he has nothing left to give him. As he came from his mother’s womb, so he must go back, naked as he came. He will take nothing from all his hard work that he can carry in his hand. This too is a painful misfortune: just as he came, so he must go. And what does he gain from toiling for the wind? All his days he eats in darkness, with much vexation, sickness and anger. This is what I have seen to be good and fitting: for people to eat and drink and enjoy all their hard work under the sun during the few days of life God has given them, for that is their share. And whenever God grants people riches and property, and lets them eat from it, take up their share and be glad in their hard work, that is God’s gift. Such people will not dwell much on the days of their lives, because God keeps them busy with gladness of heart.

fields.title: Ecclesiastes 6
fields.body_html:
Wealth without enjoyment

I have seen a misfortune under the sun that lies heavy on human beings: God gives some people wealth, possessions and honor, so that they lack nothing they desire, yet God does not enable them to enjoy it; instead a stranger enjoys it. This is a breath and a grievous sickness. A man may father a hundred children and live many years; but however many the days of his years, if his soul finds no satisfaction in good things, and he does not even receive a burial, I say that a child born dead is better off than he is. For it comes as a breath and goes into darkness, and in darkness its name is hidden. It has never seen the sun or known anything, yet it has more rest than that man. Even if he lived a thousand years twice over but did not enjoy what is good, do not all go to the same place? All people’s hard work is for their mouths, and yet their appetite is never filled. What advantage do the wise have over fools? And what does a poor person gain by knowing how to conduct themselves before others? It is better to enjoy what is before your eyes than to let desire roam. This too is a breath and chasing the wind. Whatever exists has already been named, and it is known what human beings are: they cannot argue their case against one stronger than they are. The more words there are, the more breath there is; what does anyone gain from that? For who knows what is good for people during the few days of their life, a mere breath, which they pass like a shadow? And who can tell them what will happen under the sun after they are gone?

fields.title: Ecclesiastes 7
fields.body_html:
Better than

A good name is worth more than fine perfume,
and the day of death more than the day of birth.
It is better to go to a house of mourning
than to go to a house of feasting,
because death is the end of everyone,
and the living will take it to heart.
Grief is better than laughter,
for a sad face can be good for the heart.
The hearts of the wise are in the house of mourning,
but the hearts of fools are in the house of pleasure.
It is better to listen to a wise person’s rebuke
than to listen to the song of fools.
For like thorns crackling under a pot
is the laughter of a fool.
This too is a breath.
Oppression can drive a wise person mad,
and a bribe corrupts the heart.
The end of a matter is better than its beginning,
and patience is better than pride.
Do not let your spirit be quick to anger,
for anger makes its home in the heart of fools.
Do not say, “How is it that earlier days were better than these?”
It is not wisdom that prompts that question.
Wisdom is good along with an inheritance,
and an advantage to those who see the sun.
For wisdom shelters as money shelters,
but this is the gain of knowledge:
wisdom keeps alive those who have it.
Consider what God has done:
who can straighten what he has made crooked?
When times are good, enjoy the good,
and when times are bad, consider this:
God has made the one as well as the other,
so that no one can find out anything about what is to come.
In my brief life, which is only a breath, I have seen it all: there are righteous people who perish in spite of their righteousness, and there are wicked people who live long in spite of their evil. Do not be too righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why destroy yourself? Do not be too wicked, and do not be a fool. Why die before your time? It is good to hold on to the one and not to let go of the other, for whoever fears God will come through with both. Wisdom makes a wise person stronger than ten rulers in a city. Indeed, there is no one on earth so righteous that they always do good and never sin. Also, do not take to heart everything people say, or you may hear your servant cursing you. For you know in your heart that you yourself have often cursed others. All this I have tested by wisdom. I said, “I will be wise,” but wisdom was far from me. What exists is far off and very deep. Who can find it out? I turned my mind to understand, to explore, and to search out wisdom and the reason of things, and to understand that wickedness is folly and foolishness is madness. I find something more bitter than death: the woman who is a trap, whose heart is a net and whose hands are chains. Whoever pleases God will escape her, but the sinner will be caught by her. Look, this is what I have found, says the Teacher, adding one thing to another to find the sum, which I have kept searching for but have not found. One man among a thousand I have found, but a woman among all these I have not found. This alone I have found: God made human beings upright, but they have gone looking for many schemes.

fields.title: Ecclesiastes 8
fields.body_html:
Wisdom before a king

Who is like the wise? Who knows how to explain a matter? Wisdom makes a person’s face shine and softens its hard look. I say: obey the king’s command, because of the oath you swore before God. Do not be in a hurry to leave his presence, and do not take part in a bad cause, for he does whatever he pleases. The word of a king carries supreme power; who can say to him, “What are you doing?” Whoever obeys the command will come to no harm, and a wise heart will know the right time and the right way. For there is a right time and a right way for every matter, though a person’s trouble lies heavy on them. For no one knows what is to come, and who can tell anyone how it will happen? No one has power over the wind to hold it back, and no one has power over the day of death. There is no release from that war, and wickedness will not rescue those who practice it. All this I have seen as I gave my mind to everything that is done under the sun, while one person has power over another to that person’s harm. Then I saw the wicked buried. They used to come and go from the holy place, and they were forgotten in the city where they had done such things. This too is a breath. Because the sentence against an evil deed is not carried out quickly, people’s hearts are set on doing evil. Though a sinner does evil a hundred times and lives a long life, I still know that it will go well with those who fear God, because they fear him. But it will not go well with the wicked, and their days will not grow long; they are like a shadow, because they do not fear God. There is something on earth that is a breath: there are righteous people who get what the wicked deserve, and there are wicked people who get what the righteous deserve. I said that this too is a breath. So I commend joy, for there is nothing better for people under the sun than to eat and drink and be glad. That will stay with them in their hard work through the days of life that God gives them under the sun. When I set my mind to know wisdom and to see the work that is done on earth, where people get no sleep day or night, then I saw all that God has done: no one can find out the work that is done under the sun. However hard people work to search it out, they will not find it. Even if the wise claim to know it, they cannot find it out.

fields.title: Ecclesiastes 9
fields.body_html:
One fate for all

So I took all this to heart and examined it all: the righteous and the wise and what they do are in God’s hand. Whether it will be love or hate, no one knows; everything lies ahead of them. It is the same for everyone: one fate comes to the righteous and the wicked, to the good, to the clean and the unclean, to those who offer sacrifices and those who do not. As it is with the good, so it is with the sinner; as it is with those who swear oaths, so it is with those who are afraid to swear. This is the wrong in everything that is done under the sun: the same fate comes to all. The hearts of people are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that, they go to the dead. But whoever is joined with all the living has hope, since a living dog is better off than a dead lion. For the living know that death will come, but the dead know nothing. They have no more reward, for even the memory of them is forgotten. Their love, their hate and their envy have long since perished, and never again will they have a share in anything that is done under the sun. Go, eat your food with joy, and drink your wine with a glad heart, for God has already approved what you do. Let your clothes always be white, and do not let your head lack oil. Enjoy life with the wife you love, all the days of your brief life, a breath, which God has given you under the sun, all your days that pass like a breath. That is your share in life and in the hard work you do under the sun. Whatever your hand finds to do, put all your strength into it, for in Sheol, where you are going, there is no work and no planning, no knowledge and no wisdom.

Time and chance

Again I saw under the sun that the race does not go to the fastest, nor the battle to the strongest; food does not go to the wise, nor wealth to the clever, nor favor to the skilled. Time and chance come to them all. For no one knows when their time will come. Like fish caught in a cruel net, like birds caught in a snare, so people are trapped by a time of disaster that falls on them without warning. I have also seen this example of wisdom under the sun, and it impressed me greatly. There was a small city with few people in it. A great king came against it, surrounded it and built great siegeworks against it. Now there lived in it a poor man who was wise, and by his wisdom he saved the city. Yet no one remembered that poor man. So I said, “Wisdom is better than strength.” But the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and no one listens to his words. The quiet words of the wise are heeded more than the shouting of a ruler among fools. Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but a single sinner can ruin a great deal of good.

fields.title: Ecclesiastes 10
fields.body_html:
A little folly

Dead flies make the perfumer’s oil stink and go bad;
so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.
The heart of the wise leans to the right,
the heart of a fool to the left.
Even when fools walk along the road, they lack sense,
and they show everyone that they are fools.
If the ruler’s anger rises against you,
do not leave your post,
for calmness can lay great offenses to rest.
There is an evil I have seen under the sun, the kind of error that comes from a ruler: Folly is set in many high positions, while the rich sit in lowly places. I have seen slaves on horseback, while officials go on foot like slaves.
Whoever digs a pit may fall into it,
and one who breaks through a wall may be bitten by a snake.
Whoever quarries stones may be injured by them,
and whoever splits logs is put in danger by them.
If the ax is blunt and its edge is not sharpened,
more strength must be used;
but wisdom brings the gain of success.
If the snake bites before it is charmed,
there is no gain in being a charmer.
The words of a wise person’s mouth win favor,
but fools are swallowed up by their own lips.
The words of their mouths begin with folly,
and their talk ends in harmful madness.
A fool keeps on talking,
though no one knows what is to come,
and who can tell anyone what will happen after them?
The hard work of fools wears them out,
for they do not even know the way to town.
Woe to you, land, when your king is a boy
and your officials feast in the morning!
How blessed you are, land, when your king is of noble birth,
and your officials eat at the proper time,
to gain strength and not to get drunk.
Through laziness the roof beams sag,
and through idle hands the house leaks.
Feasts are made for laughter,
and wine makes life merry,
and money answers every need.
Do not curse the king even in your thoughts,
nor the rich even where you sleep,
for a bird in the sky may carry off your words,
and a winged creature may report what you said.

fields.title: Ecclesiastes 11
fields.body_html:
Send your bread on the waters

Send your bread out on the surface of the waters,
for after many days you will find it again.
Give a share to seven, and even to eight,
for you do not know what disaster may come on the earth.
When the clouds are full of rain, they pour it out on the earth;
and whether a tree falls to the south or to the north,
wherever the tree falls, there it will lie.
Whoever keeps watching the wind will never sow,
and whoever keeps looking at the clouds will never reap.
Just as you do not know the path of the breath of life
into the bones in a pregnant woman’s womb,
so you do not know the work of God,
who makes all things.
Sow your seed in the morning,
and in the evening do not let your hands be idle,
for you do not know which will prosper, this or that,
or whether both alike will turn out well.
Light is sweet, and it is good for the eyes to see the sun. However many years a person may live, let them enjoy them all, but let them remember that the days of darkness will be many. All that comes is a breath. Be glad, young man, while you are young, and let your heart give you joy in the days of your youth. Follow the ways of your heart and what your eyes see, but know that God will call you to account for all these things. So banish anxiety from your heart and put away pain from your body, for youth and the prime of life are a breath.

fields.title: Ecclesiastes 12
fields.body_html:
Remember your Creator

Remember your Creator in the days of your youth,
while the days of trouble have not yet come
and the years have not drawn near when you will say,
“I find no pleasure in them,”
before the sun grows dark, and the light,
and the moon and the stars,
and the clouds return after the rain,
on the day when the guards of the house tremble
and the strong men stoop,
when the women who grind stop because they are few,
and the women who look through the windows see only dimly,
when the doors on the street are closed
and the noise of grinding fades,
when people rise at the sound of a bird,
and all the songs grow faint,
when people are afraid of heights and of dangers on the road,
when the almond tree blossoms and the grasshopper drags itself along,
and the caper-berry no longer stirs desire,
because everyone goes to their eternal home,
and mourners go about in the streets,
before the silver cord is snapped
and the golden bowl is broken,
before the jar is shattered at the spring
and the wheel broken at the well,
and the dust goes back to the earth it came from,
and the spirit returns to God, who gave it.
Breath upon breath, says the Teacher. Everything is a breath. Besides being wise, the Teacher also taught the people knowledge. He weighed and studied and arranged many proverbs. The Teacher sought to find pleasing words, and to write honestly words of truth. The words of the wise are like goads, and the collected sayings are like nails driven firmly in; they are given by one shepherd. Beyond these, my son, take warning: the making of many books never ends, and much study wears out the body. Here is the end of the matter, now that all has been heard: Fear God and keep his commandments, because this is the whole of being human. For God will bring every deed into judgment, including everything hidden, whether it is good or evil.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Here is the end of the matter, now that all has been heard: Fear God and keep his commandments, because this is the whole of being human. For God will bring every deed into judgment, including everything hidden, whether it is good or evil.

— Ecclesiastes 12:13–14

After twelve chapters of searching, the book ends in two sentences. They do not take back anything the Teacher said. Everything under the sun is still a breath; the wise still die like fools; the righteous still sometimes perish in their righteousness. But the frame steps forward and sets all of it inside something larger. God is, and God will judge. So the one thing that remains, when every other gain has blown away, is to fear him and keep his commandments. That, the book says, is “the whole of being human”.

It is a surprising place to arrive. The Teacher had complained that no one remembers those who came before, that the wise are forgotten as quickly as fools. The last verse answers him: God will bring every deed into judgment, “including everything hidden”. Nothing is lost to him. What looked like a breath is weighed after all.

The question the book leaves with you

Ecclesiastes asks every reader the question it asked in its third verse: what do you gain from all your hard work under the sun? It will not let you answer quickly. It has taken away the usual answers one by one: wisdom, pleasure, achievement, wealth, reputation, even a long life. None of them, held for its own sake, survives the grave.

What is left is not nothing. It is God, the giver, and his gifts, received with open hands: bread eaten with joy, work done with all your strength, life shared with the one you love, the light that is sweet to the eyes. And it is the fear of God, which holds those gifts in their place. The question Ecclesiastes leaves is whether you will build your life on what passes, or receive what passes from the hand of the one who does not.

Where Ecclesiastes points

The Teacher saw that God had “put a sense of eternity in their hearts”, and that no one could see the whole of God’s work. He could not see past the grave. The New Testament claims that someone has. The Son of God came under the sun, shared our flesh and blood, worked with his hands and wept at a friend’s tomb, and died; and by his death he set free “those whom the fear of death kept enslaved their whole life long” (Hebrews 2:15). On the third day he rose.

That is why Paul can write to people whose lives were as brief as anyone’s: “What can be seen lasts only a while; what cannot be seen is eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18). Ecclesiastes does not give that answer. It clears the ground for it, so that when the answer comes, it is heard for what it is.

Where to go from here

Ecclesiastes has spoken to preachers and thinkers in every age, often to the restless and the disillusioned. Some of the best of what they wrote is in this library:

  • On “Breath upon breath” (Ecclesiastes 1:2). John Chrysostom’s sermon Against Eutropius, preached over a fallen court minister who clung to the altar of the church he had attacked.
  • On the crooked things God has made (Ecclesiastes 7:13). Thomas Boston’s The Crook in the Lot, on bearing the hard places of a life as God’s work.
  • On a world that is a breath. John Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress, whose Vanity Fair takes its name partly from Ecclesiastes (11:8); and Hannah Whitall Smith’s chapter “Ecclesiastes: The Vanity of the World” in Old Testament Types and Teachings.
  • On the restless heart. Augustine’s Confessions, which opens with the prayer that our heart is restless until it rests in God; and Blaise Pascal’s Pensées, whose section on the misery of man without God says that Solomon and Job have best known and spoken of it.
  • On numbering our days. Jeremy Taylor’s The Rule and Exercises of Holy Dying, which begins with the vanity and shortness of human life and turns it into daily preparation for death.
  • For reading with children. Tell Me the Story – Book 9: Songs and Wise Words, an Ochorus Original, with chapters on a time for everything (3:1) and remembering your Creator (12:1).

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Ecclesiastes in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

And then read the book again, perhaps alongside Proverbs, whose confidence it tests, and the Gospels, whose good news it prepares for. The Teacher, for all his honesty about the dark, never stopped noticing the light:

Light is sweet, and it is good for the eyes to see the sun.

— Ecclesiastes 11:7
